metadata.title: Will AI Replace My Test Scripts?
metadata.narration_policy: Narration is SCRIPT.md verbatim, one script section per beat. Beat IDs B01-B11 match script sections 1-11; BVDT, BHTF and BOUT are sections 12, 13 and 14. Source tags, stage directions and the 'Prompt shown on screen' line are not narrated.
metadata.visual_policy: Simple illustrative graphics only: a mock web page, a popup with an ×, locators, a test's find, act, check steps, a look, decide, act, check loop. No real product logos, no screenshots of commercial tools, and no employer details. Code on screen is real, readable Selenium/JUnit API, labelled as illustrative and not run. The Claude composer, verdict page and the channel mark are redrawn bookends, not screenshots.

fill_policy.gate: Gate V (final_frame_check.py): content bounding box must cover at least 55% of the safe area at 50% and at 85% of every beat.
fill_policy.rule: Every Manim scene is built to fill the safe area at both sample points: large type, large objects, no top-clustered layouts. No beat is declared sparse_by_design unless a render proves it cannot pass, and then only with a written reason.

portrait_layout.rule: In 9:16, all text and labels sit above 86% of the frame height (y < 0.86 * H), leaving the bottom 14% empty. Each portrait scene has its own native layout.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Keya, and this video is about whether AI will replace my test scripts. The voice you’re hearing is an AI voice reading my script.

show.event: the ask types in under 'Hi, Keya'
three result lines land: the ID, the picture, who decides
the AI-voice disclosure is spoken while the answered composer holds

props.segment: Will AI Replace My Test Scripts?
props.command: Will AI replace my test scripts?
output: A script looks for an ID
An AI agent looks for the picture

beats.narration_text: At work, one of my test scripts kept failing. Not because the app was broken, but because a button's ID changed overnight. To close a popup, I look for the X. My script looked for an ID called close button. Now AI can test a website from plain English instructions. Should I be worried?

shot.visual_intent: A drawn web page with a popup and an × in its corner. A script window beside it looks for id="close-button"; the page's button id changes overnight and the test turns red while the page itself is fine. Then plain-English instructions point at the same page.

show.event: a code window with a few test lines draws in beside a drawn web page: 'one of my test scripts kept failing'
the test row turns red while the page beside it stays whole: the app is not broken
the popup's button id label flips from 'close-button' to a new random id overnight (moon and clock tick)
an eye marks the × in the popup corner: 'I look for the X'
the script's pointer goes to the id label 'close-button' and finds nothing: 'My script looked for an ID'
a speech bubble with plain-English instructions points at the page: 'AI can test from plain English instructions'
a large question mark lands: 'Should I be worried?'

beats.narration_text: AI won't replace testers overnight. But it will change what testers spend their time on. Let's see how, step by step.

show.event: the writer types 'AI will replace testers.' in terracotta
it pauses, then deletes the whole sentence
'AI will change what testers spend their time on.' types in ink
the corrected sentence holds while the voice says 'Let's see how, step by step'

AI will change
what testers spend
their time on

beats.note: Beat 3 per Keya: typed 'AI will replace testers.' then corrected to 'AI will change what testers spend their time on.' The whole sentence is the trigger phrase so the correction replaces the sentence, not one word (ai-explainer: correct the sentence, not just the word). The corrected sentence is typed over three lines (line breaks replace spaces) so it fits inside the title-safe margin at a large size. Verify after render: the corrected sentence is fully on screen before the cut; portrait uses BrutalistHesitantWriter916 with larger type over more lines. Check beat media against the ai-explainer 8 s floor once audio exists.

beats.narration_text: First, what is software testing? Before an app reaches you, someone checks that every button and page works. Doing that by hand, every day, is slow. So testers write test scripts: small programs that click through the app automatically.

shot.visual_intent: A drawn app page with several buttons and a second page. A cursor checks them one by one, slowly, with a clock ticking, day after day. Then a script window takes over and the same clicks run by themselves.

show.event: a drawn app opens: a login button, a menu, a form, a second page; 'someone checks that every button and page works'
a cursor clicks each element in turn and ticks it off; a calendar flips through days: 'by hand, every day'
the ticking slows and a heavy 'slow' label lands on the clock
a script window draws in beside the app: 'test scripts: small programs'
the cursor now moves on its own, clicking down the page while the ticks run quickly

beats.narration_text: Selenium is a tool that lets a script control a web browser. JUnit is the framework that runs those scripts as tests. Every test does three things: find an element, act on it, then check the result. Find the login button, click it, check that the page says welcome. To keep things tidy, each page's locators live in one place, called a page object.

shot.visual_intent: Three layers: a script drives a drawn browser (label 'Selenium'), a framework box runs the script as a test (label 'JUnit'), and a short readable Java test with find, act and check lines lit one at a time. A page-object box then gathers the locators in one place. The code is illustrative and not run; it is labelled so on screen.

show.event: a script window and a drawn browser: an arrow from script to browser, label 'Selenium: a script controls a browser'
a framework box wraps the script beside them: 'JUnit: the framework that runs the script as a test'
readable test code appears (about 30 px effective at 4K): findElement, click, assertEquals
line 1 lights, labelled FIND: 'Find the login button'
line 2 lights, labelled ACT: 'click it'
line 3 lights, labelled CHECK: 'check that the page says welcome'
a box labelled 'page object' pulls the locators out of the tests into one place: 'each page's locators live in one place'
a small note: 'Illustrative code, not run.'

beats.note: The Java is the standard JUnit 5 / Selenium WebDriver API (By.id, findElement, click, getText, assertEquals). It is shown as an illustration and was not executed, because no browser, Selenium or JUnit install is available in this toolkit; it says so on screen.

beats.narration_text: Scripts find elements by locators, like an ID. In one project, the IDs kept changing between builds, so I had to combine them with other attributes. Every time a locator broke, I had to investigate, find the new one, update it and run the test again. Across hundreds of tests, that cycle becomes unsustainable.

shot.visual_intent: A locator is an ID. Three builds of a page, the same button with a different ID each time. The fix combines the ID with other attributes. Then the repair cycle: investigate, find new, update, rerun, drawn as a loop, multiplied by a grid of hundreds of tests.

show.event: a locator tag appears on a drawn button: id="close-button"; 'scripts find elements by locators, like an ID'
three builds in a row: the same button with a different id each build; the later two turn the test red
the locator becomes id + text + class chips: 'combine them with other attributes'
a four-step loop draws: investigate, find the new locator, update, run again; a red mark starts the loop
the loop is copied into a grid of a hundred small tests, many red
the whole grid is stamped 'unsustainable'

beats.narration_text: Tools like the open-source Healenium save a working locator. When it breaks, they score the elements on the page, use the best match, and report it, so a person can fix the script.

shot.visual_intent: Healenium (text label only, no logo) saves a working locator. The locator breaks; the elements on the page get illustrative score bars with no numbers; the best match is used; a report card lists the broken and healed locators so a person can fix the script.

show.event: a label 'open-source Healenium' (text only); a drawn button with its working locator id="close-button" saved into a small store
the page changes and the locator breaks: a red cross over id="close-button"
the page's elements light as candidates, each with an illustrative score bar; no numbers
the best-scoring element is used and the test carries on
a report card lands: broken locator, healed locator, a flag 'check this'
a cursor hovers over the script's old locator line, ready for the person to edit it: 'so a person can fix the script'

beats.narration_text: Vision-based AI agents go further. They test the way a person does. To close a popup, I look for the X. Selenium looks for an ID. An AI agent takes a screenshot, finds the X by how it looks, clicks it, then takes another screenshot to check. Look, decide, act, check, again and again.

shot.visual_intent: Two lanes against the same popup. Selenium lane: looks for an ID and finds none. Agent lane: a screenshot frame, the × found by how it looks, a click, another screenshot. A ring labelled look, decide, act, check turns again and again.

show.event: a drawn popup with an ×; 'vision-based agents test the way a person does'
top lane: 'Selenium looks for an ID' with a locator tag and a stuck cursor
bottom lane: a screenshot frame snaps around the page and a ring lands on the ×
the cursor clicks the ×; the popup closes; a second screenshot frame snaps for the check
a ring with four labels, look, decide, act, check, lights one at a time
the ring turns again: 'again and again'

beats.narration_text: This idea isn't completely new to me. As an RPA developer, I built bots that could click on screen elements by how they looked, not just by their code. What AI agents add is deciding what to do next.

shot.visual_intent: A bot cursor clicks a target matched by its look, not its code. A decision fork is then added: what AI agents add is deciding what to do next. No product logos.

show.event: a drawn desktop window; 'RPA developer: bots that click on screen elements'
a small picture of a button is matched in the window by its look; the bot cursor clicks it; the code behind it is greyed out
'not just by their code' lands beside the greyed code
a fork opens after the click: three possible next steps
the agent picks one: 'what AI agents add is deciding what to do next'

beats.narration_text: AI is genuinely useful here. In my experience, it can suggest edge cases I might miss and help write test documentation, and it can keep scripts running when the page changes.

shot.visual_intent: Three helpful jobs as three drawn cards under the stamp 'In my experience': suggest edge cases, help write test documentation, keep scripts running when the page changes.

show.event: a stamp 'In my experience' (Keya's own account, not a sourced claim) lands at the top
card 1: a short test list grows by one new line marked as the edge case a person might miss
card 2: a document page writes itself line by line: 'test documentation'
card 3: a page changes shape and the green test line keeps running

beats.narration_text: But it has limits. Every run costs money. It can make different choices on different runs. It can hallucinate, and worst of all, it can heal to the wrong button and still say the test passed. And if an AI decides both what to test and whether it passed, who checks the AI?

shot.visual_intent: Four limits drawn as small panels: each run costs money, the same test makes different choices on different runs, it can hallucinate, and it can heal to the wrong button and still say the test passed. Then the closing question: who checks the AI?

show.event: panel 1: a coin meter ticks up with every run: 'every run costs money'
panel 2: the same test run twice makes two different choices: 'different choices on different runs'
panel 3: a made-up button is drawn on the page where none exists: 'hallucinate'
panel 4: the × is replaced by a wrong button, 'Buy', and the test still shows a green PASS: 'heal to the wrong button'
the AI decides what to test AND whether it passed: both arrows come from the same box
a large 'Who checks the AI?' lands

beats.narration_text: So, will AI replace my test scripts? I don't think so. AI is an addition to automation, not a replacement. It makes my work quicker and more reliable, but a human still decides what correct looks like. Even this video was built by an AI agent, and I approved every step.

show.event: the artifact page opens on the title
the heading lands: an addition, not a replacement
the closing line lands on 'I approved every step'

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Here's a Selenium test with a fragile locator. Suggest a more stable one, and explain what a self-healing tool and an AI testing agent would each do if it broke, using closing a popup as the example. And next time a test fails, ask: did the app break, or did the page just change?
